DNS & LB Lookup

Resolve a list of host names or IPs against your configured DNS servers and, in the same step, find which FortiWeb server policy or FortiADC virtual server publishes them — with links to the policy, DNS record management and a guarded service decommission.

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministrator
🔑 Permissionsnetwork.view users.manage operations.apply appliances.apply
📍 WherePlugins → DNS Lookup (every ADOM it is ticked for; the plugin dns-lb-lookup, URL /apps/dns-lb-lookup; the page also answers at /dns-lookup/)

What is it?#

DNS & LB Lookup takes up to 50 host names or IP addresses and answers two questions at once:

  1. What does DNS say? — each entry is resolved with dig against every DNS server configured for this site.
  2. Who publishes it? — each entry is matched against the load-balancing configuration of the fleet: FortiWeb server policies (from SATOM's cache) and FortiADC virtual servers (read live).

From a match you can open the policy, manage DNS records in an external DNS backend, or decommission the whole service.

It is a plugin#

Changed on 2026-11-09: DNS Lookup is a plugin. Its menu entry is Plugins → DNS Lookup, the app dns-lb-lookup 2.x, and it draws this page exactly — same form, tables, dialogs and Copy texts — because its own view is the page's template. How it is built is in Plugin Studio → Apps → DNS Lookup: the View tab is the page, the Diagram is its back end (search, live health, SPO Regex), and two more apps answer its dialogs: DNS Records (dns-records) and Delete (dns-decommission). See an app's own view.

Because Delete is the app dns-decommission, a step you add to its diagram after Apply the confirmed plan runs on every Delete — for example a call to your DDI's API through a Plugin Studio connection (see Add a step to every Delete below). The page also still answers at /dns-lookup/; it has no menu entry of its own.

What does it do?#

  • Resolves each entry against each enabled DNS server (A by default; reverse lookup for IPs; name TYPE for another type such as CNAME). A wildcard *.example.com is probed as example.example.com.
  • Shows LB matches as rows of the results table, one per match (the entry and its DNS answers span them): Gateway, Server Policy / Virtual Server, Service IP / name — the PTR name of the service IP, asked of every enabled resolver (a FortiWeb VIP's /32 is dropped first) — and Backends, each with its configured status (green enable, red disable, amber maintain).
  • Actions on each match: Show opens the whole match — product, ADOM, HTTP/HTTPS service, pool, members, certificate CN, SNI, WAF policy, App ID, the full comment, status, zone, line, department, the AppID facts and each backend — with Check live health (FortiWeb) asking the device for each backend's health-check state (UP / DOWN / no health check); Edit opens the policy; Delete starts the decommission (preview first).
  • Show AppID columns adds the AppID catalog's visible columns (named as on the AppIDs page) to the table.
  • Quick LB shows only the gateway(s).
  • Copy DNS / Copy LB copy tab-separated results for a spreadsheet. Copy LB is the full row of each match: the entry, every column, the PTR name, each backend with its status, the AppID facts and where the AppID came from.
  • Lists entries Not found in any source.
  • DNS Records (administrators) — list, create, edit and delete records in a configured DNS backend (EfficientIP SOLIDserver, phpIPAM or NetBox).
  • Decommission — plan and execute the removal of a service: its DNS records, the server policy / virtual server, SNI membership, certificate, WAF profile and carve-outs, with a preview first.

Requirements#

  • At least one DNS server configured in Administrator → Objects → DNS Resolvers (none are shipped). Until then the page says No DNS servers configured.
  • For FortiWeb matches: harvested configuration (the page reads the cache).
  • For DNS Records: a DNS backend in Settings → Integrations → DNS Records.

Permissions#

🔑Permission

  • Lookup (opening the page): network.view; all system profiles have it. Without it the sidebar link is hidden and the page answers 403. Results are limited to the appliances of the current ADOM (Global sees all).
  • DNS Lookup — resolver servers (opens Administrator → Objects → DNS Resolvers) and DNS Records: users.manage (Administrator). The button and link are hidden otherwise; the endpoints return 403.
  • Decommission: the legacy config_write gate (e.g. operations.apply or appliances.apply); the button only appears for FortiWeb and FortiADC matches.

ℹ️Note

Changed in 2.11.0: DNS & LB Lookup now requires network.view instead of sign-in alone.

How to use#

Look up names#

  1. Open Operations → DNS Lookup.
  2. Paste entries into Hostnames / IPs — one per line (optionally name TYPE).
  3. Choose Options: Lookup (Automatic, Element, IP, FQDN), Show LB matches (default on), Quick LB (gateway only), Exact match, Show TTL, Show AppID columns.
  4. Click Search. Reset clears the form.
  5. The table has a column Entry (how it was looked up and Matches: N), one column per DNS server with its answers, then Gateway, Server Policy / Virtual Server, Service IP / name (the VIP and its name), Backends and Actions; the entry spans its matches. An entry with no match is one row that says Matches: 0. The chevron (or Expand all) opens a match's data as a Field | Value table under the row — where the entry was found, every field, the pool's members.
  6. On a match, Show opens every detail (the long comment too); Check live health asks the FortiWeb for each pool member's health; Copy copies that match. Edit opens the policy in a new tab.

How an entry is searched. Automatic decides per entry:

You type SATOM does Service IP / Name
An element (a policy, pool, certificate, comment…) Searches the configuration text. The policy's VIP / the PTR of that VIP.
An IP address Searches the address fields of every server policy — VIP, pool members and any other address field of the policy, its virtual server and its pool — as a whole address ({ip} does not find {ip}). Matched on names the field. The VIP / its PTR.
An FQDN Resolves it (A and AAAA, every resolver), searches each address like an IP, and the name in the configuration text (SNI, certificate CN). The VIP / the FQDN you gave.

Automatic checks IP or FQDN first: an entry the DNS servers answer with addresses is searched by those addresses even when it does not look like an FQDN (an underscore, an internal suffix).

An empty Name always says why: no PTR, PTR error, no resolver configured or no service IP. A name that does not resolve says so, and a resolver timeout or error is shown as a DNS error. No service IP comes with the reason: only the config layer is cached (a deep capture resolves the virtual server's VIPs), the policy has no virtual server, or its interface has no address in SATOM's copy. A VIP that uses its interface address is read from the cached interface; a virtual server VIP is the address of its system vip object, never its name.

SPO Regex: the policy's name is its FQDN#

Many sites name a server policy after the service it publishes (spo_www_example_com_443). SPO Regex (button under Search) turns that name into the FQDN with ordered rules: a Pattern (regular expression, case-insensitive), a Result (\1, \g<name>; empty = the group named fqdn, else group 1, else the whole match) and Underscores to dots. The first rule that yields a valid FQDN wins; at most 10.

  1. Click SPO Regex, then Add rule, e.g. pattern ^spo[-_](.+?)(?:[-_](?:80|443|https?))?$, result \1, Underscores to dots on.
  2. Under Try it the policies on the page are filled in: click Test to see each name's FQDN, or why each rule gave none.
  3. Save (needs Manage users; audited as dns_tool.spo_regex) and search again.

With rules, an FQDN finds the policy named after it (Matched on: SPO name (SPO Regex)), even when it does not resolve or resolves to an address that is not the VIP (NAT, a CDN in front); a lookup by policy name shows its FQDN and the address it resolves to under Service IP / name. Copy LB has a SPO Regex FQDN column.

Clusters. A server policy cached on several members of one HA cluster or config-sync group is shown once, with a Cluster: name (primary node, N members) badge, so Edit, Delete and the live check act on that member only. Membership comes from the cluster registered in SATOM (node 0 and its members), else from SATOM's copy (system_ha with the same group name, or FortiWeb system_conf_sync naming another registered FortiWeb). The primary is the role recorded in SATOM — nothing is asked of the device — so when no role is recorded the badge says role unknown and the first member by name is shown.

Backends. Every match shows its pool and members (address:port, weight, configured status) from SATOM's copy; a FortiADC member's address comes from its real server. Check live health lists every member the FortiWeb reports with its health, including members missing from SATOM's copy, and shows each step (copy, question to the device, answer). Copy LB carries Lookup, Matched on, Cluster and SPO Regex FQDN; the PTR column is Name.

Manage DNS records (administrators)#

  1. Click DNS Records in the Results header.
  2. Choose the Backend (if several are configured), enter Name (FQDN), Zone, View as offered by the backend, and click Load.
  3. Edit a record or fill Type, Value, TTL and click Save record; New clears the form. Delete from the list.

Decommission a service#

  1. On a match, click Delete in Actions. SATOM builds a plan: every object that would be deleted, kept or unbound, with warnings.
  2. Read the plan. If it carries warnings, tick I have read the warnings above and accept the shared dependencies they name.
  3. Type the policy name in type the policy name to confirm.
  4. Click Delete everything listed. Results are shown per object.

Add a step to every Delete#

  1. Plugin Studio → Connections: create an HTTP connection to the system (for example your DDI's API) with its credentials.
  2. Plugin Studio → Apps → Decommission a service → Diagram: after the step Apply the confirmed plan (key apply_now) and before the Output Done, add a step such as Call an API on that connection; the decommission's result is {{ decommission }}, what was asked {{ form.policy }}, {{ form.hostname }}.
  3. Publish. The next Delete in DNS Lookup runs it, as the person who clicked, with its own line in the run's steps.

Configuration#

Field Description Required Example
Hostnames / IPs One per line; characters outside letters, digits, space and . : * _ - / are removed; max 50 entries Yes www.example.com
Show LB matches Match each entry against LB configuration No on
Quick LB (gateway only) Show only the gateway column No off
Exact match Whole-value (or comma-separated token) match instead of substring No off
Show TTL Append (TTL:n) to DNS answers No off
Show AppID columns Add the AppID catalog's visible columns to each match No off
SPO Regex Ordered rules (pattern, result, underscores to dots, on) turning a policy name into its FQDN; console-wide No ^spo[-_](.+?)(?:[-_]443)?$ → \1, dots on

DNS servers (Administrator → Objects → DNS Resolvers, /dns-lookup/resolvers): a list of name + server address with an enabled flag.

Example#

🧪Example — Who serves api.example.com, and retire it

  1. Enter api.example.com, keep Show LB matches, click Search.
  2. Both DNS servers return 192.0.2.40; one match shows FortiWeb fweb-01, policy pol-api, pool pool-api with two backends.
  3. Click Delete: the plan lists the A record, the policy, its pool, the certificate (keep — also used by another policy), and the WAF profile.
  4. Type pol-api and click Delete everything listed.

Result#

  • Lookups change nothing and are not audited. Check live health is a device read and writes policy.health_probe (member count, or the refusal).
  • DNS record changes write audit entries dns_records.create, .update, .delete.
  • Every decommission attempt writes dns_decommission.apply (successful or refused). Objects are deleted in this order: DNS records, server policy / virtual server, SNI, certificate, WAF policy, carve-outs. If the policy itself fails to delete, nothing after it is attempted.

Troubleshooting#

403 when opening DNS Lookup, or the link is missing#

Your profile does not hold network.view. Ask an administrator to add it. The entry is the plugin dns-lb-lookup: if nobody sees it, it is not imported, not published, disabled, or not ticked for this ADOM (Plugin Studio → Apps → DNS Lookup → Settings).

"No DNS servers configured."#

Add servers in Administrator → Objects → DNS Resolvers (administrators).

"LB matching failed: …"#

Building LB rows failed; the DNS half still shows. Check the devices and the cache (see Device health).

A DNS cell shows "timeout", "error" or "No result"#

The server did not answer within the timeout, the query failed, or there is no record. Check the server address in Settings.

"the plan changed since you saw it — review it again before confirming."#

Something changed between preview and confirmation (for example another session bound the certificate elsewhere). Review the new plan and confirm again.

"this plan carries warnings that need an explicit acknowledgement."#

Tick the acknowledgement checkbox.

"this plan is blocked and cannot be acknowledged away."#

A blocker (for example an object that could not be read) prevents deletion. Objects SATOM could not verify are always kept, never deleted.

"the server policy did not delete — the rest of the plan was not attempted."#

The appliance refused the policy deletion; nothing else was removed after it. See the per-object results for the reason.

"No backend carries the DNS role. Configure one in Settings -> DNS Records."#

No DNS backend is configured for record management.

"N DNS backends are configured — say which one this record belongs to."#

Choose the Backend in the dialog.

Advanced#

Advanced Data sources and matching
  • FortiWeb LB rows come from the device cache (no device call); FortiADC rows are read live, read-only.
  • Matching compares the entry and its wildcard-resolved form against every column of every LB row (substring by default).
  • The App ID is the policy's binding in the AppID catalog; without one, the AppID its comment names with Analysis › AppID pattern (resolved in the catalog when it is there); without either, the token the comment carries (AppID: <token>, app-id=…, or a bracketed [APP-123]).
  • The PTR names are looked up for the matched rows only (at most 100 addresses per search), never for the whole fleet.
  • Show health reads policy/policystatus.detail on the FortiWeb, only when you press the button; a refusal (licence, authentication) is shown as an error, never as "down".
  • dig runs with a 2-second timeout and one try per server; lookups run in parallel (up to 8).
#dns#dig#lookup#hostname#load balancer match#vip#service ip#spo regex#policy name to fqdn#ptr#reverse lookup#fqdn#ip search#cluster#ha#pool members#backends#decommission#dns records#efficientip#phpipam#netbox
